content.text: # Parameters of _Stretto_ Use inside the _Contrapunctus_ 5 of the _Art of Fugue_ by Johann Sebastian Bach (BWV 1080, 5)[1](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/)All numbering in this essay regarding the works of Bach corresponds to the Schmieder catalogue (BWV). ## Parameters of _Stretto_ Use inside the _Contrapunctus_ 5 of the _Art of Fugue_ by Johann Sebastian Bach (BWV 1080, 5)[1](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/)All numbering in this essay regarding the works of Bach corresponds to the Schmieder catalogue (BWV). #### Konstantinos G. Alevizos **Abstract** In this article, my objective is to attempt to connect all the simultaneous compositional processes that J. S. Bach combined in order to create the _stretto_ forms inside the _Contrapunctus_ 5 of the _Art of Fugue_. The analysis offers a perspective by relating four technical elements present in every _stretto_ of the subject; the distance of entry in each voice, the raw material used, the technique of inversion and the position of _dux_ and _comes_. Keywords:[analysis](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/tag/Analysis/); [Johann Sebastian Bach](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/tag/Bach-Johann-Sebastian/); [compositional techniques](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/tag/Compositional-techniques/); [fugue](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/tag/Fugue/); [_stretto_](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/tag/Stretto/). **Résumé** Dans cet article mon objectif est de tenter de connecter – en traçant les liaisons – toutes les techniques compositionnelles simultanées que Bach a employé afin de créer les différentes possibilités de _stretto_ dans le _Contrapunctus_ 5 de _L’art de la fugue_. L’analyse offre une nouvelle perspective en mettant en relation quatre éléments présents dans chaque exposition du sujet en _stretto_, en essayant en même temps de discerner leur logique de disposition: la distance d’entrée, la technique d’inversion, le positionnement des _dux_ et _comes_ ainsi que l’utilisation d’éléments rythmiques spécifiques. Mots clés:[analyse](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/tag/Analyse/); [Jean-Sébastien Bach](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/tag/Bach-Jean-Sebastien/); [fugue](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/tag/Fugue/); [_stretto_](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/tag/Stretto/); [techniques compositionnelles](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/tag/Techniques-compositionnelles/). When observing and studying the music of Johann Sebastian Bach,[2](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/)I do not use the term “listen” only because much of these examination fields are not apprehended during the listening process. we may find ourselves at an impasse due to the presence of several parallel, but connected, analytical fields. The difficulty of simultaneously processing several of these fields[3](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/)As an example, I could use several possible analysis approaches that can be overtaken on the structural (morphological) plan of a work, such as harmonic, rhythmic, arithmetic, rhetorical, the theological approaches, etc.makes it necessary to thoroughly and methodically examine one field before examining another. By analysing multiple facets of the music, we create a bridge of understanding among these apparently heterogeneous fields, which enables us to better comprehend the inner structure of the composition. However, these heterogeneous fields do not always interact with one another in a clear way. Despite the multiple fields of analysis, the composer may choose to focus his or her attention on one or several specific techniques in each piece. In the case of _Contrapunctus_, these are contrapuntal techniques. It is well known that Bach was interested in complex compositional procedures. However, he did not leave behind any theoretical work besides his music.Nonetheless, his attitude towards these procedures can be documented in many ways. For example, only some of the ways Bach uses numbers in his music include the total number of bars of a composition (or of the inner parts of it),[4](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/)The Prelude and Fugue in B Minor, BWV 544, employs 33 bars (not an incidental number) for the creation of an “intermezzo” inside the fugue, beginning in A major, between bars 28 and 61.the number of times that a motif is repeated inside a work,[5](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/)One example is the _Orgelbüchlein_ chorale _Vom Himmel hoch_, BWV 606, where the bass motif is repeated 14 times. The same is true for BWV 615.the total number of notes inside a specific subject, the symmetry and proportion inside a series of compositions represented by numbers,[6](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/)An example of this is the two-voice inventions in BWV 771-786. and the application of Smend’s number alphabet; there are a multitude of other ways beyond the scope of this article (Houten and Kasbergen 2003; Tatlow 1991, 2015). Furthermore, many of these studies offer different points of view regarding the use of numbers inside Bach’s music. Consequently, Bach’s music output has been examined through Pythagorean (Dentler 2000), theological (Göncz 2012) and occasionally, esoteric and symbolic lenses. The mere transliteration of numbers inside Bach’s music is of less importance than the directed use of numerical procedures for compositional reasons. The _Art of Fugue_ is a series of compositions (or a composition in the form of a series, as Spitta called it) that use many compositional techniques in different ways. Perhaps the unfinished fugue (BWV 1080, 19) is the most fertile case; the use of precise technical procedures here is undisputed[7](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/)As an example, see the research of Zoltán Göncz 2013, pp.129-130. Göncz identified the exact position of the missing fourth voice/subject for the final four-voice _stretto_. The research of Gregory Butler indicated the length of a fourth subject by investigating the proportions of the existing three. As far as the mirrored expositions inside the _Contrapunctus_ 6 are concerned, I suggest Alevizos 2016, p.210.(Göncz 2013, pp.129–130; Butler in Butler, Stauffer and Green 2008, pp.119–120; Alevizos 2016, p.210). While the research that examines the philological aspects of the work is quite abundant, equivalently detailed score analysis of the work is not available. To the best of my knowledge, the following represents the most important analytical score study of the work (Higgs 1877; Wolfgang Graeser in Bach 1926; Tovey[1931]1974; Dickinson 1950, 1956; Bitsch 1967; Chailley 1971; Wiemer 1977, 1981; Kolneder 1983; Heinrich 1983; Schleuning 1993; Vartolo 2008; Alevizos 2016). The _Art of Fugue_ is a musical work in which Bach explores different compositional techniques, which can stand separately, but are also organized in a climactic pattern from beginning to end. [8](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/)The notion of progression inside the work is not new; Heinrich (1983) based his entire conception on this matter and so did Bagnal (1975) who used this concept to reorganize the first section of the work. Lester (2001) proposed the same idea to sustain the heightening levels theory.The use of numbers can easily be found when these techniques occur, and the aim of the current essay is to demonstrate their use for specific compositional goals and the methodological procedures that Bach uses to achieve these. ### _Contrapunctus_ 5 _Contrapunctus_ 5 holds the fourth position inside the manuscript _P200_ and the fifth position inside the original editions of 1751 and 1752. Regardless of its position inside the collection, it is possible to consider this piece as an _ouverture_ to the _stretto_ technique within the entire work.[9](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/)Although _Contrapunctus_ 2 of the original edition appears to present dotted rhythmic elements (derivatives of the _codetta_ of the subject), it is known than Bach elaborated the score a second time by adding the dots to transform it into a dotted form, as Wiemer (1981) has demonstrated.This fugue differs from the fugues in the first section (fugues 1 to 4); beginning with this fugue, Bach clearly introduces the _stretto_ technique in addition to inversion and reversion[10](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/)To the best of my knowledge, James Higgs was the first to document the difference between the inversion and reversion of a subject inside the _Art of Fugue_, especially regarding the “mirror” fugues. Through these means, the interval inversion of a subject differs from its voice position (reversion) inside a fugue. In a reversion, the voices are exchanged around the center axis of the score (_i.e._ soprano becomes bass, alto becomes tenor; see Higgs 1877, pp.63-64).(Higgs 1877, p.63). Inverted and reverted triple counterpoint are also used in some cases (Alevizos 2016, p.210).However, Bach seriously addresses these last two compositional methods separately, namely, inside the third section (in the double fugues 9 and 10 and triple fugues 8 and 11) and fourth section (inversion and reversion, fugues 11 and 12) of the _Art of Fugue_. In this second section of the work (fugues 5, 6 and 7), the basic element on which the composer focuses a great deal of his attention is the _stretto_. _Contrapunctus_ 5 has a rather regular overall form, with a tendency towards symmetry. This can be seen by examining the global structure of the fugue, which consists of alternating expositions and episodes and connecting sections and canons in a rather regular and coordinated manner (Alevizos 2016, p.309). Based on this morphological plan of the fugue, it is possible to affirm that in this fugue, Bach carefully planned the distance of entry of each subject exposition. The overall structure can be divided in three parts (the first part is in the tonic, the second part is a harmonic elaboration, and the third part is a re-exposition) without insinuating any meaningful link to the classic tripartite form. The use of a tripartite structure could be explained as a rhetorical gesture (Levarie and Merrick 1943, pp.16–17). These formal decisions suggest a clear premeditated effort in the construction of the fugue. However, as far as the morphological plan of the fugue is concerned, it is possible to acknowledge parallel compositional techniques with heightening levels of activity throughout the piece. It is not possible to confirm the same arrangement for the _stretti_ overall sequence (as we will see in the next pages). In addition, the fugue includes two four-part canonical episodes, which can be interpreted as a premonitory indication of the importance _stretto_ will acquire in the following fugues of the collection.[11](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/)Although I do not intend to discuss the global structure and the ordering procedure inside the _Art of Fugue_, it is quite clear that Bach used the subjects of _Contrapunctus_ 1 and 5 as basic subjects. Furthermore, inside the progressive order of the series of all fugues, Bach introduced elements of technique inside earlier fugues for exhaustive exploitation in later fugues.Therefore, after having accepted the progressive and accumulative predisposition of the _Art of Fugue_ as a whole (Heinrich 1983, p.3), it is easy to understand that the premeditation process accounts for not only the creation of _Contrapunctus_ 5, but also its position and significance inside the entire sequence of fugues. Technically, the entire fugue is based on three types of raw material, specifically the dotted rhythm of the subject, the _codetta_ and the rhythmic element of the anapaest (the two eighth-notes followed by a quarter note). [![Image 1: Figure 1: Contrapunctus 5, bars 1-5, alto.](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/figure-1.bmp)](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/figure-1.bmp) _Figure 1:_ Contrapunctus _5, bars 1-5, alto._ We distinguish the dotted rhythm (bars 1–3) in the first part of the subject, the _codetta_ in the second part (bar 4), and the anapaest in bar five. Among the first five fugues, this is the first time that Bach exploits many elements simultaneously (however, not insistently) inside a fugue. His habitual way of proceeding in the first section of the _Art of Fugue_ consists of elaborating a single element. In _Contrapunctus_ 5, the first of the second section, Bach elaborates on several elements: the _stretto_ and the inversion techniques, the anapaest segment of the countersubject and the syncopation effect, and the _codetta_ and the dotted segment of the subject. Figure 2 presents the global morphological structure of _Contrapunctus_ 5. Beyond the choice of the raw material to elaborate (rhythmic segments, etc.) or Bach’s compositional methods (syncopation, inversion, etc.), this structure shows the way in which he conceived the distribution of the thematic phases within the fugue. Figure 2 is a comprehensive source of information regarding the construction of each thematic phase and its arrangement within the fugue. The table also indicates the position and structure of the episodes and canons (Ep./Can.), the harmonic scale of each exposition of the subject, and the direction of each subject (_rectus_**↑**or _inversus_**↓**) and its function as _dux_ or _comes_. Furthermore, this table allows us to examine the internal construction of each thematic phase. A risk of interpretation exists in compiling this table because of the occasional difficulty in selecting which subject expositions to place together. Here, I attempted to consider different aspects to obtain the most accurate view of the whole. Two principal aspects create unity among apparently detached subject expositions, namely, the position of each voice inside a specific thematic phase and its distance of entry. [![Image 2: Figure 2: Comprehensive morphological structure of Contrapunctus 5.](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/figure-2-998x1024.jpg)](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/figure-2.jpg) _Figure 2: Comprehensive morphological structure of_ Contrapunctus _5._ Additionally, the harmonic development of the fugue differs from its morphological development, which means that the harmonic modulations do not necessarily correspond to the progression of the thematic phases. Consequently, different types of exposition can belong to the same harmonic setting, which is the case for the thematic phases in F, G and B≅ (bars 33–52).[12](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/)The same operation occurs between bars 57 and 90, in which the harmonic setting is the same, but the structure of each thematic phase is different.These subject expositions create a unity as expositions that are not in the tonic harmonic setting, and they use a different approach in terms of the distance of entry and the technique of inversion but have a similar progression method (_dux_ and _comes,_ DDCD). Therefore, it is clear that to advance the understanding of the combinations among the thematic phases, it is necessary to define the basic principles of elaboration that Bach uses when he provides a specific identity to an exposition. Accordingly, it is possible to list the following elements: 1. Harmonic field of the subject and its environment; 2. _Stretto_ (distance of entry); 3. Technique of inversion; 4. Raw material; and 5. Subject/Answer(_dux_/_comes_). These elements are possible criteria that might have helped organize the specific _stretto_ combinations. ### The _Stretto_ Possibilities Donald Francis Tovey affirmed that the subject of the _Art of Fugue_ was designed for the fugues of the second section (5, 6 and 7) and especially for _Contrapunctus_ 5 (Tovey[1931]1974, p.10). This is indeed true because it enabled the composer to work livelier _stretto_ possibilities than the _stretto_ arrangements that use the subject in its simple state (_Contrapunctus_ 1). Additionally, it gives the composer the opportunity to work with more clarity with reversible counterpoint (Franck 2010, pp.121–122; Bitsch and Bonfils 1981, pp.12–13; Mann 1987, p.271). The rhythmic structure of the simple subject (_Contrapunctus_ 1) does not allow voices to be heard as clearly in complex _stretto_ constructions due to its homogeneous rhythmic nature, which is based entirely on half notes. In contrast, the dotted subject (_Contrapunctus_ 5) offers an immense variety of _stretto_ possibilities and inversions. Regarding the use of inversion in the _Art of Fugue_, Bach creates a pivot key (normally the mediant of the scale) around which the intervals are inverted. In this way, he retains the inverted construction inside a harmonic setting without the need to modulate. [![Image 3](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/figure-3.bmp)](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/figure-3.bmp) _Figure 3: The creation of inversions._ Accordingly, while inverting a subject in this way, any interval can be reproduced on the pivot as a quantity and not necessarily as a quality (a quantity is simply an interval number without an interval quality, such as major or minor). Therefore, it is possible to understand that when a _rectus_ subject in D minor modulates to A minor with the elevation of G to G# (in the dominant of A minor), its inversion will not necessarily involve the flattening of E. If this were the case, then the flattening of the E key (in E b) would create a Neapolitan sixth or at least an environment in which modulation occurs towards the subdominant scale (IVth degree).Accordingly, the inversion works in the context of a single scale; otherwise, its use could create unwanted harmonic modulations. To avoid unnecessary modulations, the interval’s quality is always tied to the harmonic function in a given section. In the _Art of Fugue_, Bach uses two types of _stretto_. The first type of _stretto_ is used within the second section (fugues 5, 6 and 7), and is the most appealing and complex _stretto,_ following a note-by-note procedure when combining phrases. The second type of _stretto_ combines larger subjects (including the altered subjects of the _Art of Fugue_[13](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/)The subjects of fugues 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 and 19, excluding the canons, are altered.), which cannot be combined by using complex juxtaposition procedures. Therefore, to appreciate the most interesting use of the _stretto_ inside the _Art of Fugue_, it is necessary to acquire a synoptic awareness of the second section of the work. The construction of the subject of the fugue permits many possible _stretto_ arrangements with different entry intervals.[14](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/)In the annex of the present article, I present four comprehensive tables that include the _stretto_ combinations of the subject in RR, II, RI and IR. The problems of the diminution and augmentation of the subject are addressed inside fugues 6 and 7. Moreover, exhaustive research on the _stretto_ combinations demands the possibility of juxtaposing the subjects as _dux_ or _comes_ due to the alteration of the first note in the tonal responses.However, in the present fugue, Bach does not choose to create _stretto_ expositions with a shorter entry-distance than that of a half note, apart from the two canon episodes. Consequently, the patterns are always multiples of half notes (half note, half note x2, x3, x4, x5 and x6, _i.e._, the half note, whole note, dotted whole note, etc.), although in this fugue, he does not use the double whole note as an entry distance. However, not all _stretto_ combinations are possible, even with Bach’s seemingly careful planning. The problem appears when the juxtaposition occurs between the leading tone (C# in the tonic scale) and the first degree (D) or in the inverted setting, between the sixth (B b in the tonic scale) and the dominant (A) degree. The tables included in the annex can provide a more precise overview on the issue regarding the impossibility of some _stretto_ combinations. Figure 4 shows three _stretto_ combinations that are not possible due to the creation of harmonic dissonances. The same result occurs in the inverted setting of these three _stretti_ (on the mediant) with the conversion of C# and D to B b and A, respectively. Thus, the reversion (reversing voice order and inverting melodic content) of the settings given in Figure 4 cannot be used either. These include the sequence of II (inversus-inversus) with a half note entry distance, II at the double whole note and IR (inversus-rectus) at the dotted whole note. [![Image 4: Figure 4: Non-operational stretto combinations.](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/figure-4-1024x780.jpg)](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/figure-4.jpg) _Figure 4: Non-operational_ stretto _combinations._ However, Bach invents a solution to soften the harmonic dissonance of some _stretto_ combinations that could not have worked with the original subject of _Contrapunctus_ 1. By adding dotted values to the plain subject, he creates passing notes that can resolve the harmonic dissonance. This is not always true from a strict and theoretical point of view, because the dissonant value is usually larger than the consonant value, whereas the opposite should be the case. Nonetheless, this provides a workable solution to the problem. [![Image 5: Figure 5: Avoiding dissonance in the stretto combinations of the dotted subject.](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/figure-5-1024x475.jpg)](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/figure-5.jpg) _Figure 5: Avoiding dissonance in the_ stretto _combinations of the dotted subject._ The first _stretto_ of Figure 5 presents a combination of two entries of the plain subject with an entry distance of a whole note. This subject is probably unusable in this fugue[15](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/)Bach reveals all the _stretto_ possibilities of the dotted subject progressively but mostly in _Contrapunctus_ 7, where he presents the _stretti_ in “Rectus, Inversus, per Augmentationem et Diminutionem” and in its normal state for three voices and in reversion.due to the harmonic dissonance of the augmented fifth (F-C#) and the diminished fourth (C#-F), which creates a particularly harsh effect on the strong beat. In the second example, Bach, by using the dotted subject, succeeds in evading the first dissonant interval by using the passing note E, which creates a major sixth (E-C#) when the F resolves down. Theoretically, a problematic situation remains because the dissonant interval has a greater value than the consonant one, but to the listener, it sounds resolved. The entire collection of fugues is filled with examples of this _appoggiatura_ effect, which lends itself to a double interpretation depending on the note that needs to resolve. [![Image 6: Figure 6: The two methods of the appoggiatura effect.](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/figure-6-150x150.jpg)](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/figure-6.jpg) _Figure 6: The two methods of the appoggiatura effect._ Whether the F resolves to the E or the C# resolves to the D depends on the composer’s choice to create a dominant or tonic harmony. Thus, without the appoggiatura effect, some _stretto_ combination are impossible to use without harmonic dissonance. ### Examination of the _Stretto_ in _Contrapunctus_ 5 In _Contrapunctus_ 5, Bach creates six separate exposition groups that all use a clearly-defined combination pattern regarding the distance of entry inside each _stretto_ group. Bach did not conceive the global setting of the fugue as a continuous _stretto_ device, so he did not feel the necessity to progressively decrease the distance of the subjects’ entries. This explains the non-progressive (non-decreasing) _stretto_ behaviour of the thematic phases (Tovey[1931]1974, p.11). In fact, after the second exposition group (bars 33–45), which employs the half note as an entry distance, Bach uses the dotted whole note for the exposition group that follows (bars 47–62). The continuously decreasing _stretto_ distances, as in a typical fugue stretto structure, only begins in bar 72 with the use of eighth notes in the bass line. This also explains the non-typical use of the tenor twice inside a single thematic phase (bars 69–77). In this case, Bach decides to sacrifice the correct order of the voices in the S – T – A – B exposition by changing the order to S – T – A – T. This allows the melodic line of the bass to take auditory precedence inside the beginning of the _stretto_ progression, compared to the voice entry. It appears that Figure 2 creates more questions than it resolves, mainly because the morphological structure of the fugue can be defined in many ways according to the principle that underlies the division, and the most common principle is the entry distance of the voices. Moreover, this principle automatically considers the matching of the position of the voices in each exposition group. The third, fourth and fifth expositions (Figure 2) simultaneously consider the correct position of the voices and the entry distance but do not match the inversion symmetry. This is because expositions 1, 2 and 3 use an alternating method regarding the inversion (↓↑↑↓ – ↓↑↓↑ – ↑↓↓↑ or IRRI – IRIR – RIIR), but beginning from exposition 4 (expositions 4 and 5), the inversion occurs in parallel pairs ↓↓↑↑ – ↓↓↑↑. Therefore, it is necessary to admit the impossibility of combining three elements that may have defined the structure of the expositions, specifically, the entry distance, voice position and inversion. I could extend this operation by examining the presence of a possible systematic arrangement of _dux_ and _comes_ inside the exposition groups, a puzzle that Chailley (1971) attempted to resolve regarding the entire _Art of Fugue_. In this way, the coexistence of four elements would create an even more complex combination system. However, regarding the _dux_ and _comes_, the plan appears to be quite conceivable; the fugue is divided into two parts: one part that uses the DDDC (and in mirror, CDDD) combination (expositions 1 and 2), and another part that uses the DDCD combination (expositions 3, 4 and 5). [![Image 7: Figure 7: Combination of the four elements.](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/figure-7.bmp)](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/figure-7.bmp) _Figure 7: Combination of the four elements._ Apparently, the combination of these four elements does not provide any satisfying pattern that suggests a system or a premeditated method of composition regarding the fugue. However, this demonstrates the composer’s careful consideration in parallel and simultaneous technical fields of exploration within the compositional process. Principally, Bach applies systematic procedures at different levels (fields) of the composition without implying a premeditated interconnected structure between these levels. The parts that unify the structure of _Contrapunctus_ 5 probably do not interact isomorphically with these elements. Although the existence of a compositional method that encompasses the entire series of fugues seems possible, it is thus difficult to say that the same is true for the construction of each fugue. This is not necessarily the case because it does not exist but rather because it is very difficult to recognise. Regarding this last issue, many important and indisputable discoveries have been made in recent decades that have examined precise technical procedures. These include the presence of the segmented countersubject in _Contrapunctus_ 2 within the so-called simple fugues (Rivera 1978, p.345), the transformation to the dotted theme in the same fugue (Wiemer 1981, p.416), the study of proportions regarding the length of the unfinished fugue (Butler 1983, p.56), the compositional plan of the same fugue (Göncz 1991, p.115), and the presence of mirrored entries inside _Contrapunctus_ 6 (Alevizos 2016, p.210). All of these works identify a precise technique or systematic plan that aims at a specific result, while also exploiting the use of arithmetical and compositional procedures. Nevertheless, in attempting to identify the reasons that led the composer to one choice over another regarding the use of a specific technique, we are led to considerations of the composer’s subjective choices. The use of elaboration of the _stretto_ forms inside this _Contrapunctus_ of the _Art of Fugue_ is not a mere application of an extra-musical concept that enters the musical score through numbers. This _stretto_ use is but one of many compositional techniques that have a specific musical goal, which is achieved through different levels of the compositional process. Although it is quite difficult to identify these goals, I believe that Bach’s aim is to profoundly elaborate different contrapuntal structures inside his compositional system, which he mentally categorized. Accordingly, the _stretto_ technique (as a categorised type of contrapuntal virtuosity) is examined thoroughly to create a precise set of inherent constructive elements that can be identified and elaborated. Bach, in this way, consolidated for posterity some of the most essential rudiments of counterpoint technique. ### Bibliographie Alevizos, Konstantinos (2016), _L’art de la Fugue de Johann Sebastian Bach,_ Saarbrücken, EUE. text:
# The Well-Tempered Clavier I No. 3 in C-sharp major – Bach

It is the most impossible key in the whole of the [_Wohltemperirte Clavier_](/en/bwv/?aob_facet_series_ids=4): C-sharp major. No fewer than seven sharps adorn the beginning of each staff. Furthermore, it is an unnecessarily complicated key, as instead of seven sharps you could use five flats to write exactly the same pitch – as D-flat major. In 1728, the music theorist Johann David Heinichen therefore classified C-sharp major as one of the ‘superfluous keys’. Here, Bach is deliberately toying with the mind of the keyboard player, as the instinctive correspondence between the black noteheads on the paper and the fingers on the keys no longer works.

In 1728, Johann David Heinichen wrote that it was ‘completely unorthodox’ to compose in F-sharp major and C-sharp major. And years later, in 1795, another writer thought that these keys were suitable for ‘the horror of secret Persian sultans or demons’. They were keys that existed ‘on the borders of the musical world”. C-sharp major did indeed remain extremely rare for many years after Bach’s day. And then, of course, there is the question of how C-sharp major could anyway sound ‘well-tempered’. Difficult, mysterious and problematic, in other words.

Yet the Prelude is a model of melodious simplicity and the Fugue has one of the liveliest themes of the whole _Wohltemperirte Clavier_. Bach was clearly more in line with Johann Mattheson, who predicted in 1719 that in a couple of hundred years’ time musicians would be playing C-sharp major just as easily as the village organists of the time played C major.

**[Das Wohltemperirte Clavier, BWV 846-893](/en/bwv/?aob_facet_series_ids=4)  
**Composing 48 keyboard pieces in all 24 keys was the sort of challenge Bach enjoyed. In each of the two parts of the _Wohltemperirte Clavier_, he brought together the musical couple prelude and fugue 24 times; twelve in minor keys and twelve in major. In the preludes, he gave free rein to his imagination, and demonstrated mathematical tours de force in the fugues. In contrast to the iron discipline Bach had to apply to his church compositions, here he could abandon himself to intellectual _Spielerei_ without worrying about deadlines.

The first part of the _Wohltemperirte Clavier_ dates from 1722, although it contains some music that was written in the preceding five years. There is less clarity about the history of part two. Bach compiled this second manuscript only around 1740, although once again some of the preludes and fugues it contains date from a much earlier period. Bach described the target group for this collection of pieces as follows: ‘Zum Nutzen und Gebrauch der Lehr-begierigen Musicalischen Jugend, als auch dere in diesem studio schon habil seyenden besonderem ZeitVertreib’ (For both the education of the industrious musical youngster and the enjoyment of those well-versed in this material’).

text:
# Analysis of Bach's Fugue BWV 846 in C major (WTC I)

This fugue in C major, the first fugue from the first book of Bach's _Well-Tempered Clavier_, presents several interesting aspects:

*   The voices appear in the exposition in the unusual order of subject - answer - answer - subject.
*   After the exposition Bach presents numerous _stretti_ without any interruption.
*   The only measures where the subject is not present are measure 23 and the two last measures of the fugue.

Some authors propose various numerological symbolism. The 14 notes long subject is said to be related to Bach's name:

![](../../../res/images/articles/BWV846/sujeto.gif)

> B = 2, A = 1, C = 3, H = 8  
> 2 + 1 + 3 + 8 = 14

It is also said that the subject appears exactly 24 times in this fugue representing the 24 fugues in the first book of the _Well-Tempered Clavier._ But as you will see in our analysis, there are only 22 complete subjects. To be able to get to the total of 24 subjects you need to include two incomplete presentations of the subject. The first incomplete appearance is in measure 14:

![](../../../res/images/articles/BWV846/01.gif)

The 4 last notes are missing, yet this voice enters in a _stretto_, so you really hear it as a subject entrance even if the 4 last notes are missing.

The second incomplete appearance is in measure 15 where only the first 7 notes are presented:

![](../../../res/images/articles/BWV846/03.gif)

In the third incomplete appearance in measure 20, we only hear the first 3 notes (although you may find some relations between the sixteenth notes in the next measure with the 32ths notes of the subject):

![](../../../res/images/articles/BWV846/02.gif)

It is up to you to decide...

arguments.content:
# Role A History / Primary-Source Report — Preset 07 “Stretto Engine”

**Phase:** 10.2 composer-informed arrangement presets  
**Role:** A — artist/style historian and primary-source researcher  
**Reference:** selected fugues by Johann Sebastian Bach, not “Bach style” generally  
**Retrieval date for all web sources:** 2026-07-19  
**Method boundary:** abstract descriptions only; no themes are reproduced.

## Executive judgment

The catalog sentence **“tonic, fifth, and octave answers enter progressively closer”** can honestly reference a *bounded modern arrangement assembled from historical fugal vocabulary*: entries of one recognizable subject at tonic- and dominant-related pitch levels, octave/register redistribution, and successively shorter entry delays. It must **not** be presented as a rule of Bach’s fugues, as a literal reconstruction of any selected fugue, or as evidence that Bach routinely made stretto progressively denser toward the end. A corpus study of all forty-eight *Well-Tempered Clavier* fugues found no strong support for conclusion, quantity, or progressively smaller-onset hypotheses and directly contradicted the density hypothesis; a detailed analysis of *Art of Fugue*, Contrapunctus 5 likewise describes its global stretto distances as non-progressive. [McDonald 2020](https://uwo.scholaris.ca/items/90e7593a-4d35-4969-a861-833fd36ed166); [Alevizos 2019](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/). **Confidence: high.**

The defensible reference corpus is deliberately narrow:

1. **WTC I, Fugue in C major, BWV 846/2** — an unusually concentrated early Leipzig/Cöthen-derived stretto fugue preserved in Bach’s 1722 fair copy, useful for close entries at varied temporal and pitch intervals.
2. **WTC I as a controlled corpus (BWV 846–869)** — not to claim uniform practice, but to locate BWV 846/2 within a pedagogical collection whose autograph was revised over time.
3. ***The Art of Fugue*, Contrapunctus 5, BWV 1080/5** — late, explicitly systematic exploration of stretto with rectus/inversus, dux/comes, multiple entry distances, and carefully managed contrapuntal compatibility.
4. **The forty-eight WTC fugues only as corpus-level negative evidence** — to test, and reject as a generalization, the simple “ever closer = climax” story.

This selection spans a 1722 collection and the late 1740s project only where source records support dating. It does not imply a straight career ladder from “simple” to “complex.”

## 1. Scope and corpus

### 1.1 BWV 846/2: concentrated stretto in WTC I

Bach’s autograph collective manuscript **D-B Mus.ms. Bach P 415** contains WTC I; Bach Digital identifies J. S. Bach as scribe, dates the source exactly to **1722** from title page and handwriting, notes later revision evidence, and lists BWV 846/2 in the source. The institutional item record places BWV 846 on fols. 2v–4r and the fugue heading on f. 3v. [Bach Digital, source 00001361](https://www.bachdigital.de/receive/BachDigitalSource_source_00001361); [Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek, BWV 846 item](https://www.deutsche-digitale-bibliothek.de/item/4XMMG7JXF6O2WULOOGWJFRRTABJFSQGT). **Confidence: high.**

Score-based summaries agree on the salient procedure: following the exposition, BWV 846/2 presents numerous overlapping entries, at varied time and pitch intervals, with very little non-subject material. Kerman calls it a stretto fugue fitting roughly two dozen entries of a one-and-a-half-bar subject into 27 bars and stresses that the stretti occur at many time and pitch intervals. [Kerman 2005, ch. 1, DOI landing page](https://doi.org/10.1515/9780520962590-004). Teoria’s score analysis locates incomplete/contested subject-like entries at mm. 14, 15, and 20 and warns that the familiar “24 subjects” count depends on what fragments are admitted; it counts 22 complete statements and treats further fragments as analytical choices. [Rodríguez Alvira 2005](https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/BWV846/). **Confidence: high for dense stretto and varied intervals; medium for any exact total because entry boundaries are disputed.**

Responsible entry references usable by the synthesis:

- **mm. 1–7:** four-voice exposition, with tonic-level subject and dominant-level answer functions distributed through the voices.
- **from m. 7:** overlapping entries begin; one published score-analysis inventory identifies the m. 7 treble/tenor pair as a tonic-level entry followed by a dominant-level answer in stretto.
- **mm. 14–15 and m. 20:** fragmentary entries demonstrate that “entry” counts are analysis-dependent; do not encode “24” as historical fact.
- **m. 23 and final two measures:** Teoria reports these as the only measures without the subject, reinforcing the work’s exceptional saturation.

The measure references are analytical navigation aids, not a claim that all editions phrase or label fragments identically.

### 1.2 WTC chronology and transmission

WTC I’s title page says the collection was made for the use of inquisitive musical youth and the recreation of those already skilled; this supports an exemplary/pedagogical context, not a public concert-cycle origin. [DDB, P 415](https://www.deutsche-digitale-bibliothek.de/item/RRRM6XIGAGPM7T77HOEB5MEGYWAHLDIP). The 1722 fair copy is an **autograph**, but “1722” is not a safe date for first composition of every constituent movement: the Netherlands Bach Society notes that Part I includes material written during approximately the preceding five years. [Netherlands Bach Society, BWV 848 context](https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-848). P 415 also bears evidence of later attention; therefore “autograph fair copy” should not be flattened into “unchanged first version.” **Confidence: high.**

WTC was circulated in manuscript during Bach’s life; complete printed editions appeared only around **1801**, independently through firms including Simrock, Nägeli, and Hoffmeister/Kühnel. Those prints are reception evidence, not witnesses equal in authority to P 415 for Bach’s 1722 text. [Yo Tomita, Simrock chronology](https://www.qub.ac.uk/tomita/essay/simrock/); [Henle, WTC I publication history](https://blog.henle.de/en/2022/10/31/if-thats-not-reason-enough-to-celebrate-300-years-of-wtc-i/). **Confidence: high.**

### 1.3 Late corpus: *The Art of Fugue*, especially Contrapunctus 5

Bach Digital distinguishes two source states rather than one fixed “final masterpiece”:

- The **autograph-score version**, BWV 1080.1, survives in **D-B Mus.ms. Bach P 200** and is dated **1742–1749** from watermark and handwriting; earliest traces of the subject occur in contrapuntal studies with Wilhelm Friedemann Bach around 1736–39. [Bach Digital, autograph version](https://www.bachdigital.de/receive/BachDigitalWork_work_00001266).
- The **original-print version**, BWV 1080.2, rests on engraving models from about **1747–48**; Bach changed ordering and added material, but the first edition appeared posthumously around the end of **1751**, with a second printing in spring 1752. [Bach Digital, print version](https://www.bachdigital.de/receive/BachDigitalWork_work_00011581).

Thus P 200 is an autograph primary source, while the 1751 print is a posthumous edition with pre-death authorial preparation but an editorial/publication history after Bach’s death. They differ in ordering and content. Contrapunctus 5 is fourth in P 200 but fifth in the original print. Any measure citation must name the movement, not infer an invariant cycle position. **Confidence: high.**

Alevizos’s peer-reviewed score analysis identifies Contrapunctus 5 as an opening into the collection’s concentrated stretto procedures. It analyzes six exposition groups through four independent parameters: entry distance; rectus/inversus orientation; dux/comes function; and voice position/raw material. Crucially, the entry distances do **not** form a single decreasing series: after a very close group in **mm. 33–45**, the following group in **mm. 47–62** is wider; a more continuously decreasing passage begins only around **m. 72**. [Alevizos 2019](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/). **Confidence: high for the cited analysis; medium for claims of Bach’s compositional intention beyond what the score demonstrates.**

## 2. What “stretto” historically means

In fugal usage, *stretto* (Italian, “close/narrow”) means that a subsequent statement of the subject or answer begins before the preceding statement has finished, or at a shorter temporal distance than in the opening exposition. The decisive property is **temporal overlap/close imitation of thematic statements**, not simply thick texture, faster tempo, more notes, or voices playing in parallel. Nineteenth-century definitions already distinguish fugal stretto from the tempo-direction sense of *stretto/stringendo*. [Grove’s *Dictionary of Music and Musicians*, “Stretto”](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/A_Dictionary_of_Music_and_Musicians/Stretto); [Prout, *Fugue*, ch. 8](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Fugue_%28Prout%29/Chapter_8). **Confidence: high for the technical distinction; medium as evidence for Bach’s own terminology because these definitions postdate him.**

Bach left no treatise defining his stretto practice. The historically safer approach is to describe score relations—onset distance, overlap, pitch level, subject/answer function, inversion, augmentation/diminution—rather than claim that Bach himself named each passage “stretto.” [Alevizos 2019](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/). **Confidence: high.**

## 3. Historical and aesthetic context

Fugue was not a rigid fill-in-the-form template. Its shared vocabulary included a subject, imitative entries, tonic/dominant answer relations, contrapuntal combination, episodes, sequences, cadence, inversion, augmentation/diminution, and sometimes stretto. Stretto is therefore a **technique within fugue**, not a compulsory terminal section.

Within WTC I, BWV 846/2 makes close thematic combination nearly the governing texture. The collection’s title-page pedagogy and systematic traversal of tonalities support hearing this fugue as an exemplary demonstration of contrapuntal possibility. Yet adjacent WTC fugues pursue different formal and affective problems; BWV 846/2 is not a miniature of all Bach fugues.

In *The Art of Fugue*, a common subject is subjected across separate contrapuncti to changing technical problems. Contrapuncti 5–7 intensively explore stretto alongside inversion and, later, augmentation/diminution. In Contrapunctus 5, the dotted rhythmic form helps certain overlapping combinations remain contrapuntally workable; Alevizos shows that not every imaginable offset is usable because particular collisions create unwanted dissonance. This is selective compositional design, not mechanical stacking. **Confidence: high.**

## 4. Evolution without a false ladder

A simple story—“1722 Bach uses basic stretto, late Bach perfects it by entries getting ever closer”—is unsupported.

- **WTC I / BWV 846/2 (1722 fair copy):** already exceptionally concentrated and varied. Its close entries do not await a late-career discovery.
- **WTC across both books:** McDonald’s 48-fugue corpus study reports no strong evidence that stretto passages become more numerous, more crowded, or temporally closer near fugue endings; density results directly oppose the standard hypothesis. [McDonald 2020](https://uwo.scholaris.ca/items/90e7593a-4d35-4969-a861-833fd36ed166).
- **Late *Art of Fugue*:** the project is more explicitly systematic across a cycle, but Contrapunctus 5’s actual onset distances are locally reordered rather than monotonically compressed. Its distinctiveness lies in coordinated exploration of multiple parameters and subject transformations, not merely “more voices sooner.”

The evolution is therefore best described as **changing project context**: concentrated local construction in one WTC fugue; broad variety across a pedagogical collection; and later, collection-wide comparison of contrapuntal procedures in *The Art of Fugue*. **Confidence: high.**

## 5. Persistent traits versus work-specific procedures

### Persistent across the selected evidence

- A recognizable subject remains intelligible under overlapping entry.
- Entry timing and pitch level are structural variables, not random echo settings.
- Independent lines preserve contrapuntal viability; density is constrained by what the subject can combine with.
- Tonic/dominant relations coexist with register redistribution and other tonal levels.
- Stretto can articulate continuation, return, demonstration, or climax; its function depends on placement.

**Confidence: medium-high:** recurring in the selected corpus, but not claimed for every Bach fugue.

### Specific to BWV 846/2

- Near-continuous subject saturation after the exposition.
- Very little episode space and no stable countersubject in the usual sense.
- Entry counts complicated by fragments at mm. 14–15 and 20.

**Confidence: high.**

### Specific to Contrapunctus 5 / *Art of Fugue*

- Coordinated rectus/inversus and dux/comes combinations.
- A dotted subject form whose rhythmic detail enables particular close combinations.
- Six analyzed exposition groups with non-monotonic global entry distances.
- Placement within a larger sequence that later extends stretto into diminution and augmentation.

**Confidence: high for score relations; medium for teleological readings of the cycle.**

## 6. Shared fugue vocabulary versus characteristic choices

| Shared eighteenth-century fugal vocabulary | Characteristic choices in this corpus |
|---|---|
| Tonic subject and dominant answer | BWV 846/2’s unusually sustained, episode-poor thematic saturation |
| Subject transferred among registers/voices | Its many offsets and pitch intervals within only 27 measures |
| Close imitation and invertible counterpoint | Contrapunctus 5’s systematic intersection of entry distance, inversion, and dux/comes |
| Episodes, cadence, modulation | Deliberate omission/reduction of episodes in BWV 846/2; differently grouped expositions in Contrapunctus 5 |
| Inversion, augmentation, diminution | Collection-scale isolation and recombination of these techniques in *The Art of Fugue* |

Calling every tonic/dominant imitation “Bach-like” mistakes common vocabulary for authorship. What is defensibly characteristic here is the **economical, technically tested recombination of a subject with itself under varied constraints**.

## 7. Exact judgment on the catalog claim

### What it can honestly reference

1. **“Tonic … answers”** — repeated subject statements at the tonic level, historically better called subject/dux entries rather than all “answers.”
2. **“Fifth … answers”** — dominant-level comes/answer relations central to fugal exposition and present in BWV 846/2. The engine may use a literal perfect-fifth transposition only as a simplification.
3. **“Octave … answers”** — the same thematic material redistributed to another voice/register at octave equivalence. This describes register/voice placement, not a third harmonic answer category parallel to tonic and dominant.
4. **“Enter progressively closer”** — an audible arrangement trajectory made by shortening successive onset delays; this is compatible with some local stretto progressions and with the historical meaning of “closer.”

### What it must not claim

- That tonic, fifth, and octave are Bach’s fixed three-entry recipe.
- That a tonal answer is always an exact perfect-fifth transposition; tonal answers may alter intervals to preserve tonic/dominant function.
- That “octave answer” is a standard function equivalent to dominant answer.
- That all entries must start on only those pitch classes; Bach’s later entries can occur at varied tonal levels.
- That closer entry distance automatically produces valid Bachian counterpoint. Contrapunctus 5 demonstrates unusable combinations and deliberate rhythmic/harmonic adjustments.
- That Bach’s fugues normally tighten monotonically or reserve stretto for a final climax.
- That a two-to-four-note live motif reproduces the long-range harmonic, voice-leading, inversion, and formal planning of the cited works.

**Recommended honest label text:** “A strict-canon arrangement inspired by Bach’s varied stretto practice: repeated motif entries at tonic-, dominant-, and octave-related placements arrive at shorter delays. It is not a reconstruction of a Bach fugue.”

## 8. Common caricatures and myths to avoid

1. **“Stretto means faster.”** False in fugal usage: it concerns entry spacing/overlap; a separate tempo-direction meaning exists.
2. **“Stretto always comes at the end to create climax.”** A traditional textbook tendency, contradicted by early and distributed stretti and by the WTC corpus result.
3. **“Closer is always more Bachian.”** False. Subject design, dissonance treatment, voice leading, and harmonic function constrain workable combinations.
4. **“Every Bach fugue follows exposition–episode–stretto.”** Fugue is procedurally diverse; BWV 846/2 is exceptional precisely because its subject saturation leaves almost no episode space.
5. **“Twenty-four entries in BWV 846/2 is settled fact.”** The total depends on admitting incomplete statements; Teoria identifies 22 complete entries and several fragments.
6. **“The Art of Fugue was published by Bach as a final fixed sequence.”** False. Autograph and posthumous print versions differ; dating, ordering, and completion history must remain distinct.
7. **“Bach invented tonic/dominant answers and stretto.”** False; these belong to inherited fugal/imitative practice. Bach’s distinction lies in particular constructions, not ownership of the vocabulary.
8. **“Mathematical procedure makes the music automatic.”** False. Alevizos shows multiple simultaneous systems that do not collapse into one simple numerical plan.

## 9. Primary evidence and source hierarchy

### Primary / institutional sources retained

- **Bach Digital, D-B Mus.ms. Bach P 415** — autograph source record for WTC I, scribe, dating, contents, revisions. https://www.bachdigital.de/receive/BachDigitalSource_source_00001361
- **Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek, BWV 846 / P 415** — institutional manuscript metadata and folio/heading information. https://www.deutsche-digitale-bibliothek.de/item/4XMMG7JXF6O2WULOOGWJFRRTABJFSQGT
- **Bach Digital, BWV 1080.1 autograph version** — P 200 dating and version history. https://www.bachdigital.de/receive/BachDigitalWork_work_00001266
- **Bach Digital, BWV 1080.2 print version** — engraver-model, first-edition, second-print chronology and reordering. https://www.bachdigital.de/receive/BachDigitalWork_work_00011581

### Scholarly / score-analysis sources retained

- **Joseph Kerman, *The Art of Fugue: Bach Fugues for Keyboard, 1715–1750* (University of California Press, 2005), ch. 1** — scholarly contextual reading of BWV 846/2 and varied stretto intervals. https://doi.org/10.1515/9780520962590-004
- **Kathryn McDonald, “Exploring Stretto: An Investigation into the Use of Stretto in J. S. Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier” (Western University thesis, 2020)** — full 48-fugue corpus test and negative result for standard climax/density hypotheses. https://uwo.scholaris.ca/items/90e7593a-4d35-4969-a861-833fd36ed166
- **Konstantinos G. Alevizos, “Parameters of Stretto Use inside the Contrapunctus 5…” *Revue musicale OICRM* 6/1 (2019), 142–159** — peer-reviewed, measure-specific analysis of entry distances, inversion, dux/comes, and non-progressive global behavior. https://doi.org/10.7202/1062432ar
- **José Rodríguez Alvira, “Analysis of Bach’s Fugue BWV 846 in C major” (2005)** — public score map, useful for fragment/count disagreement; lower authority than the sources above. https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/BWV846/
- **Yo Tomita, Simrock/WTC publication chronology** — specialist source-history resource. https://www.qub.ac.uk/tomita/essay/simrock/

### Sources dropped or bounded

- **Oxford/Grove online “Fugue”** — paywalled in this run; bibliographic landing page was visible, full claim text inaccessible. Not relied upon for detailed claims.
- **Neue Bach-Ausgabe volumes/critical reports** — no stable accessible full text was obtained in this run. Bach Digital source records and institutional facsimile metadata substitute for source-state claims; this is a gap, not equivalence.
- **IMSLP user scans/modern performance editions** — useful for visual checking but not used as authority for source chronology where Bach Digital exists.
- **Wikipedia, commercial analysis sites, anonymous SEO pages** — omitted because stronger institutional or scholarly sources were available.
- **Nineteenth-century dictionary/Prout definitions** — retained only to document conventional terminology, explicitly bounded as post-Bach evidence.

## 10. Confidence, disagreements, and gaps

| Claim | Confidence | Qualification |
|---|---:|---|
| Stretto is overlapping/closer thematic entry, not merely tempo or density | High | Terminology is later codified; Bach left no definition treatise |
| P 415 is Bach’s 1722 WTC I autograph fair copy with later revision evidence | High | Individual movements can predate compilation |
| BWV 846/2 is exceptionally saturated with varied stretto | High | Exact entry total depends on fragment criteria |
| “24 entries” is disputed | High | Teoria counts 22 complete; other writers include incomplete entries |
| WTC fugues do not support a general monotonic end-tightening law | High | Based on one recent thesis corpus methodology; replication would strengthen it |
| Contrapunctus 5 has non-progressive global entry distances | High | Alevizos’s grouping is an interpretation, though measure relations are observable |
| *Art of Fugue* autograph and original print are distinct versions | High | Exact intentions for final ordering/completion remain debated |
| Tonic/fifth/octave + shrinking delays is Bach’s recipe | Rejected | It is a modern bounded abstraction only |

**Outstanding gaps:**

1. The NBA critical reports were inaccessible; editorial variants affecting particular BWV 846/2 entry readings were not collated.
2. McDonald’s repository abstract was accessible, but the full tables needed to quote exact onset-distance distributions for BWV 846/2 were not extracted. The report therefore uses the corpus conclusion, not unsupported numeric detail.
3. No claim is made about tempo, articulation, instrumentation, or performance practice; the sources do not prescribe one definitive realization.
4. Contrapunctus 7 was considered but excluded from detailed measure claims because Contrapunctus 5 had the stronger accessible peer-reviewed analysis and already tests the preset’s “progressively closer” premise.
5. Analytical labels such as incomplete subject, exposition grouping, and tonal level can differ among analysts; implementation should test audible motif identity rather than pretend those disagreements are settled.

## Conclusion for parent synthesis

**Historically defensible core:** one motif recognized across independent, overlapping entries; entry delay as a structural parameter; tonic/dominant relationship plus register redistribution; and a bounded movement from spacious to closer imitation.

**Non-negotiable approximation statement:** Preset 07 is a strict-canon interaction inspired by selected Bach stretto procedures. Its literal pitch offsets and progressive delay compression are product rules, not a model of Bach’s general fugue practice. It omits tonal-answer adjustment, subject-specific contrapuntal testing, inversion, harmonic planning, episodes, cadences, and source-specific voice leading.

**Role A decision:** **ready for parent synthesis only if the UI and implementation retain that approximation boundary; otherwise reject as misleading.**

# Role A History / Primary-Source Report — Preset 07 “Stretto Engine”

**Phase:** 10.2 composer-informed arrangement presets  
**Role:** A — artist/style historian and primary-source researcher  
**Reference:** selected fugues by Johann Sebastian Bach, not “Bach style” generally  
**Retrieval date for all web sources:** 2026-07-19  
**Method boundary:** abstract descriptions only; no themes are reproduced.

## Executive judgment

The catalog sentence **“tonic, fifth, and octave answers enter progressively closer”** can honestly reference a *bounded modern arrangement assembled from historical fugal vocabulary*: entries of one recognizable subject at tonic- and dominant-related pitch levels, octave/register redistribution, and successively shorter entry delays. It must **not** be presented as a rule of Bach’s fugues, as a literal reconstruction of any selected fugue, or as evidence that Bach routinely made stretto progressively denser toward the end. A corpus study of all forty-eight *Well-Tempered Clavier* fugues found no strong support for conclusion, quantity, or progressively smaller-onset hypotheses and directly contradicted the density hypothesis; a detailed analysis of *Art of Fugue*, Contrapunctus 5 likewise describes its global stretto distances as non-progressive. [McDonald 2020](https://uwo.scholaris.ca/items/90e7593a-4d35-4969-a861-833fd36ed166); [Alevizos 2019](https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol6-n1/parameters-of-stretto/). **Confidence: high.**

The defensible reference corpus is deliberately narrow:

1. **WTC I, Fugue in C major, BWV 846/2** — an unusually concentrated early Leipzig/Cöthen-derived stretto fugue preserved in Bach’s 1722 fair copy, useful for close entries at varied temporal and pitch intervals.
2. **WTC I as a controlled corpus (BWV 846–869)** — not to claim uniform practice, but to locate BWV 846/2 within a pedagogical collection whose autograph was revised over time.
3. ***The Art of Fugue*, Contrapunctus 5, BWV 1080/5** — late, explicitly systematic exploration of stretto with rectus/inversus, dux/comes, multiple entry distances, and carefully managed contrapuntal compatibility.
4. **The forty-eight WTC fugues only as corpus-level negative evidence** — to test, and reject as a generalization, the simple “ever closer = climax” story.

This selection spans a 1722 collection and the late 1740s project only where source records support dating. It does not imply a straight career ladder from “simple” to “complex.”

## 1. Scope and corpus

### 1.1 BWV 846/2: concentrated stretto in WTC I

Bach’s autograph collective manuscript **D-B Mus.ms. Bach P 415** contains WTC I; Bach Digital identifies J. S. Bach as scribe, dates the source exactly to **1722** from title page and handwriting, notes later revision evidence, and lists BWV 846/2 in the source. The institutional item record places BWV 846 on fols. 2v–4r and the fugue heading on f. 3v. [Bach Digital, source 00001361](https://www.bachdigital.de/receive/BachDigitalSource_source_00001361); [Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek, BWV 846 item](https://www.deutsche-digitale-bibliothek.de/item/4XMMG7JXF6O2WULOOGWJFRRTABJFSQGT). **Confidence: high.**

Score-based summaries agree on the salient procedure: following the exposition, BWV 846/2 presents numerous overlapping entries, at varied time and pitch intervals, with very little non-subject material. Kerman calls it a stretto fugue fitting roughly two dozen entries of a one-and-a-half-bar subject into 27 bars and stresses that the stretti occur at many time and pitch intervals. [Kerman 2005, ch. 1, DOI landing page](https://doi.org/10.1515/9780520962590-004). Teoria’s score analysis locates incomplete/contested subject-like entries at mm. 14, 15, and 20 and warns that the familiar “24 subjects” count depends on what fragments are admitted; it counts 22 complete statements and treats further fragments as analytical choices. [Rodríguez Alvira 2005](https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/BWV846/). **Confidence: high for dense stretto and varied intervals; medium for any exact total because entry boundaries are disputed.**

Responsible entry references usable by the synthesis:

- **mm. 1–7:** four-voice exposition, with tonic-level subject and dominant-level answer functions distributed through the voices.
- **from m. 7:** overlapping entries begin; one published score-analysis inventory identifies the m. 7 treble/tenor pair as a tonic-level entry followed by a dominant-level answer in stretto.
- **mm. 14–15 and m. 20:** fragmentary entries demonstrate that “entry” counts are analysis-dependent; do not encode “24” as historical fact.
- **m. 23 and final two measures:** Teoria reports these as the only measures without the subject, reinforcing the work’s exceptional saturation.
